chapter_theme: Listening to the wise as a form of learning open even to those who haven't studied. The chapter treats the ear as an organ of nourishment and taste, rivalling the mouth, and it softens the verdict of the previous chapter.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of listening (411-412), those who have it (413), the good it does them (414-417), and the fault of its absence (418-420).

411.reading: The wealth among wealths is the wealth of the ear; that wealth stands first among all wealth.
411.nuance: The sound does the work, with செல்வம் in every half-line. After 400 has already denied other wealth the name, this verse places the ear at the head of that revalued wealth.

412.reading: When there is no food for the ear, a little may be given to the stomach too.
412.nuance: The verse is witty, not ascetic. Parimelazhagar catches the two loaded words: சிறிது, and ஈயப்படும், which treats the stomach as a beggar to be given alms. It also says the food is given so that one can go on listening.

413.reading: Those who have listening as food for the ear, though on earth, are equal to those fulfilled by the food of oblation.

positions.position: ஆன்றார் here are the gods who receive sacrificial offerings. The listeners are their earthly equals.
ஆன்றார் are human sages who eat little and are full of understanding, with no sacrifice or gods.

414.reading: Even if you haven't studied, listen; it will be a staff to lean on in one's faltering.
414.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes that the உம்மை in ஆயினும் keeps study as the first duty. Listening is not offered as an equal path, only as what remains. He also makes the faltering inward: a mind shaken by poverty or ignorance.

415.reading: The words from the mouths of those of good conduct are like a staff on slippery ground.
415.nuance: The authority comes from the speaker's conduct, not learning. Parimelazhagar makes the exclusion explicit: the learned without conduct are not to be heard at all. So the chapter's listening is listening to a kind of person.

416.reading: Listen to good things, however little; that much too will give full greatness.

positions.position: Even a little brings full greatness. Like drops of rain, the listening accumulates, so don't despise the small.
positions.quote: அக்கேள்வி மழைத் துளைபோல வந்து ஈண்டு எல்லா அறிவுகளையும் உள ஆக்கலின்

positions.position: Greatness comes in proportion: as much as one listens, that much greatness.

417.reading: Those whose listening is gathered upon their own close investigation do not speak folly, even when they have misunderstood.
417.nuance: A subtle claim: being wrong and speaking foolishly are different things. Such a person can err and still not talk nonsense. இழைத்துணர்ந்து comes before கேள்வி, and Parimelazhagar reads this as one's own investigation first, confirmed by consulting those who know.

418.reading: Ears not pierced by listening are deaf even though they hear.
418.nuance: தோட்கப்படாத plays on pierced ears, ornament and all. Parimelazhagar's closing remark is apt: the old hole isn't a hole. Listening must make a new opening.

419.reading: It is hard for those without fine listening to have a mouth that bows.
419.nuance: The bowing is done by the mouth, so this is humility as a way of speaking. The causal claim is striking: humility comes from having listened, because those who haven't heard much admire themselves, as Parimelazhagar explains.

420.reading: What does it matter whether they die or live, these beings who know taste by the mouth and not by the ear?
420.nuance: The verse doesn't say to whom it doesn't matter; both older commentators supply the world, which makes it a social judgment of uselessness, not a cosmic one. மாக்கள் rather than மக்கள் also seems to me a deliberate demotion. It may also echo அவி of 413, oblation there and perishing here, though that is my suggestion.

links.note: The same formula, செல்வத்துள் செல்வம், is given to the wealth of the ear here and to the wealth of grace in 241. 400 adds learning. The Kural's chapters each crown their own wealth, which raises the question of how they rank.
Both use the leaning staff, but 414 has listening as the staff and 415 the speaker's conduct. Read together, the staff only holds if the one speaking has conduct.
978 says greatness bows while smallness vaunts. 419 gives that a source: the bowing mouth comes from listening, so 978's humility is partly a product of hearing.

source_issues: 411: The Manakkudavar entry is marked [#] and is close to Parimelazhagar's wording, so I did not treat it as independent.
